lesson.title: Turning the Product Rule Into a Working Formula
lesson.summary: With the product rule justified, this section turns it into a fast mechanical formula, including the extension to three or more factors multiplied together.
lesson.body:
Once the product rule has been derived, it is worth restating it as a clean formula you can apply on sight, without re deriving it every time: if h(x) = f(x)g(x), then h'(x) = f'(x)g(x) + f(x)g'(x). A common way to say this out loud is derivative of the first times the second, plus the first times the derivative of the second. The order of the two terms does not matter since addition is commutative, but keeping a consistent habit, always differentiating the first factor first, helps avoid dropping a term when a problem gets busy.

A natural question is what happens with three factors multiplied together instead of two. The formula extends by applying the two factor rule twice. Let h(x) = f(x)g(x)k(x), and group the first two factors as a single function u(x) = f(x)g(x). Then h(x) = u(x)k(x), so by the two factor product rule, h'(x) = u'(x)k(x) + u(x)k'(x). Substituting u'(x) = f'(x)g(x) + f(x)g'(x) from the two factor rule again and distributing k(x) through gives h'(x) = f'(x)g(x)k(x) + f(x)g'(x)k(x) + f(x)g(x)k'(x). The pattern is clean: differentiate exactly one factor at a time, leave the other two untouched, and add up all three versions.

A worked example shows the three factor formula in action. Let p(x) = x(x+1)(x+2), with f(x) = x, g(x) = x+1, h(x) = x+2, so f'(x) = 1, g'(x) = 1, and h'(x) = 1. Applying the extended formula, p'(x) = f'(x)g(x)h(x) + f(x)g'(x)h(x) + f(x)g(x)h'(x) = (x+1)(x+2) + x(x+2) + x(x+1). Expanding each piece: (x+1)(x+2) = x^2 + 3x + 2, x(x+2) = x^2 + 2x, and x(x+1) = x^2 + x. Adding all three gives 3x^2 + 6x + 2.

As with the two factor case, this deserves an independent check by expanding p(x) first. p(x) = x(x+1)(x+2) = x(x^2 + 3x + 2) = x^3 + 3x^2 + 2x. Differentiating term by term with the power rule gives p'(x) = 3x^2 + 6x + 2, which matches the product formula result precisely. The agreement is not an accident, it is the same underlying limit argument applied twice, just packaged into a formula that saves you from expanding messy products by hand.

It is worth being explicit about a mistake this formula invites once problems get busier: forgetting one of the terms. With four or more factors the same grouping trick keeps working, differentiate exactly one factor in each term while leaving every other factor untouched, and sum over as many terms as there are factors, but it becomes easy to lose track of one term along the way. A reliable habit is to write down a blank template first, one addition sign for every factor, before filling in any derivatives, so a missing term is obvious from the shape of the expression rather than something you have to notice after the fact.

The practical payoff of having the formula memorized this way is speed and reliability on functions that would be painful to expand, such as a product of several distinct polynomials, a polynomial times a root, or, once trigonometric derivatives are introduced later, a polynomial times a sine or cosine. In every one of those cases the formula works exactly the same way: differentiate one factor, keep the rest fixed, sum over all the factors, and you never need to multiply the whole expression out first.
